quote: We used to have more values, but it was difficult to remember them all. In response, we condensed them, created an acronym (CREDIT), and listed operating principles to guide behavior.
fact: GitLab condensed its earlier, longer list of values into the acronym CREDIT (Collaboration, Results for Customers, Efficiency, Diversity Inclusion & Belonging, Iteration, Transparency) because the old list was hard to remember.

quote: Results for Customers is at the top of our values hierarchy, as our customers achieving results drives overall business performance that enables everything else.
fact: Results for Customers is the highest value in GitLab's values hierarchy.

quote: If a change impacts Transparency positively but impacts Efficiency negatively in roughly the same amount, we would move ahead since Transparency is higher in the hierarchy than Efficiency.
fact: In the values hierarchy Transparency ranks above Efficiency, so an equal trade-off between them is resolved in favor of Transparency.

quote: Negative feedback can be given in a group setting if it's to someone higher in the management chain. This shows that no one is above feedback.
fact: Negative feedback normally goes 1-1, but it may be given in a group when it is aimed at someone higher in the management chain.

quote: team members react to a negative incident with their managers [six times more strongly](https://hbr.org/2013/03/the-delicate-art-of-giving-fee) than they do to a positive one.
fact: The values page cites that team members react six times more strongly to a negative incident with their manager than to a positive one.

quote: We are **S**hort **Te**rm **C**ritical **A**nd **L**ong **T**erm **O**ptimistic (`STeCALTO`, for short).
fact: STeCALTO means Short Term Critical And Long Term Optimistic, part of the 'Focus on improvement' operating principle.

quote: Below are 12 examples of things we've seen mistaken as iteration, but don't meet our definition of iteration.
fact: The values page lists 12 things that are not iteration, such as reducing quality, avoiding documentation, compromising on security, and imposing long hours.

quote: For example we [shipped over 133 monthly releases](https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2018/11/21/why-gitlab-uses-a-monthly-release-cycle/).
fact: Under 'Set a due date', the values page says GitLab shipped over 133 monthly releases, cutting scope rather than missing dates.

quote: The poll results showed that 100% of those polled preferred a different title and the title was changed.
fact: The 'Brag Document' was renamed after a TMRG channel poll in which 100% of respondents preferred a different title.

quote: We call this arguing against a "steel" position, instead of a "straw" one.
fact: Under 'Assume positive intent', team members should argue against the strongest ('steel man') version of an opposing position, not a straw man.

quote: In these cases, the [Directly Responsible Individual](/handbook/people-group/directly-responsible-individuals/) should go ahead and make them without approval.
fact: For two-way door (reversible) decisions, the DRI should decide without approval; only irreversible decisions need a more thorough discussion.

quote: - Environments with fast feedback (SaaS) over slow feedback (self-managed)
fact: For gradual rollouts, GitLab prefers few users over many, internal users over external, and SaaS (fast feedback) over self-managed (slow feedback).

quote: We want a **values fit**, not a culture fit.
fact: GitLab hires for values fit rather than culture fit, calling 'culture fit' a bad excuse and preferring 'culture add'.

quote: Companies are encouraged to copy and implement GitLab's values. They are Creative Commons and can be copied verbatim.
fact: GitLab's values are published under Creative Commons and other companies may copy them verbatim.

quote: which is why every promotion document at GitLab is shared with the entire company and uses the values as its core structure.
fact: Every promotion document at GitLab is shared with the whole company and is structured around the values.

quote: Providing GitLab team members and [qualified individuals](/handbook/ceo/shadow/#eligibility) transparency into all aspects of the company through the [CEO Shadow Program](/handbook/ceo/shadow/#goal) to enable them to better engage and collaborate cross-functionally.
fact: The CEO Shadow Program is listed as one of the ways GitLab reinforces its values.

quote: Apple, for example, values secrecy over transparency and product perfection over iteration.
fact: The values page uses Apple as an example of a successful company built on GitLab's counter-values: secrecy over transparency and perfection over iteration.

quote: As a [public company](/handbook/company/being-a-public-company/), we declare everyone in the company as an insider, which allows us to remain transparent internally about our numbers, etc.
fact: As a public company, GitLab declares every team member an insider so it can stay transparent internally about its numbers.

quote: From our values we excluded some behaviors that are obvious; we call them our *permission to play* behavior:
fact: 'Permission to play' is the name for obvious baseline behaviors (being honest, dependable, acting lawfully, no favoritism) that are left out of the values.

quote: Some dysfunctions are not addressed directly by our values; for example, trust is not one of our values.
fact: Trust is deliberately not a GitLab value; it is treated as an outcome that is earned.
